lines.text: LEXICON.
א
The name Aleph, like those of the
other letters, is of Phenician origin, and
signifies ox, bullock, i. q. Heb. אֶלֶף. So
Plutarch, Quæst. Sympos. IX. 2: Aleph
is put before the other letters διὰ τοὺς
Φοίνικας οὕτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν. The
name is derived from the form of this
letter in the most ancient alphabet, re-
presenting the rude outline of a bullock’s
head, still found in the remains of the
Phenician dialect: 𐤀, 𐤀, 𐤀. As a
numeral it denotes unity or 1; and with
two points above (א̈), 1000.
Of all the Hebrew gutturals Aleph
has the softest pronunciation, being ut-
tered with a slight breathing from the
throat or rather lungs, like the Greek
spiritus lenis, and the French h in habit,
homme, which we are apt to neglect,
because we cannot give them correctly.
And since by a sort of common usage in
languages, especially in those of the
Semitic family, (comp. Ewald in Heb.
Gram. § 31,) the stronger and harsher
letters in the course of time become by
degrees softened and give place to
smoother ones, we hence see why in
Aramæan, in the later Hebrew, and in
Arabic, the stronger gutturals ח and ע
are softened into א. E. g. הִתְקַטֵּל,
ܐܶܬܩܰܛܰܠ; הִקְטִיל, ܐܰܩܛܶܠ, אַקְטֵל; אָמוֹן
Jer. 52, 15 for הָמוֹן multitude, etc.
But, vice versa, א sometimes passes
over into ה and ע; and in general,
these letters, being very similar in pro-
nunciation, are very often interchanged
with one another. Comp. הֵיךְ in the
later Hebrew for the common אֵיךְ; אָבִיב
ear of grain, comp. Syr. ܗܰܒܳܒܳܐ flower;
כָּאָה and כָּהָה, לָאָה and לָהָה; also אָגַם
and עָגַם to be sad; אוּד and עוּד to turn
(both of them also in Ethiopic); גָּאַל and
גָּעַל to pollute; תָּאַב and תָּעַב to abhor;
גָּמָא and גָּמַע to suck in, to drink; פִּתְאֹם
suddenly, from פֶּתַע a moment, etc.
Where Aleph is to be still more soft-
ened, it passes over into the quiescents ו
and י, as אָחַד and יָחַד to make one; אָלַף
ܝܼܠܶܦ to learn; רְאֵם, רֵים, buffalo; בּוֹר
for בְּאֹר a well. Hence it comes, that
many verbs פ״א accord in signification
with verbs ע״ו, comp. Heb. Gr. § 76. 2;
e. g. אָדַשׁ and דּוּשׁ; אָנַשׁ, Syr. ܢܳܫ, to be
sick.
In respect to the forms of words it may
be noted: a) That א without a vowel at
the beginning of a word is often dropped
by aphæresis, as אֲנַחְנוּ, נַחְנוּ, we; אֲשֶׁר
later שֶׁ·, who, which, what; אֶחָד and חַד
one, Ez. 33, 30; הָסוּרִים for הָאֲסוּרִים
Ecc. 4, 14; comp. Lehrgeb. p. 135, 136.
b) But also at the beginning of words, a
prosthetic א is often prefixed, comp.
Lehrgeb. p. 139. See אֲבַטִּיחִים, אֲגַפִּים,
אֲבַעְבּוּעֹת, אֲדַרְכּוֹן. This is done chiefly,
where a word otherwise begins with two
consonants separated in pronunciation
only by a movable Sheva, as זְרוֹעַ, אֶזְרוֹעַ,
the arm; אֶשְׁכֹּל Aram. סְגוֹל grape (in
which both forms occur); also אֶפְרוֹחַ for
פְּרוֹחַ progeny; אֶגְרֹף for גֹּרֶף the fist;
אֶתְנָן for תְּנָן a gift; אַכְזָב for כָּזָב false.
Comp. Gr. χθές and ἐχθές yesterday,
and also similar examples in the transi-
tion from Latin to French, as spiritus,
esprit; status, état. In the Syriac man-
ner א is also added before the letter י;
as יִשַׁי and אִישַׁי Jesse, 1 Chr. 2, 12.
* אָב m. constr. אֲבִי, c. suff. אָבִיו,
אָבִיךָ, אֲבִיכֶם, 1 pers. אָבִי (from אָב);
Plur. אָבוֹת, constr. אֲבוֹת, c. suff. אֲבֹתַי,
אֲבֹתֵיכֶם, אֲבֹתָם and אֲבֹתֵיהֶם, father.
It is a primitive word, see note; and is
common to all the Semitic dialects, Arab.

line_status.note: The mark after "Plutarch" descends below the baseline with a tail, unlike the round full stops after "Quæst." and "Sympos.", so it is a comma, not a period.

The two dots over the aleph are printed side by side horizontally, as in the diaeresis-like mark for the thousands numeral; U+0308 (Reading B) represents this, whereas U+0595 zaqef gadol (Reading A) is a vertically stacked pair, which is not what is printed.

The letter after "gutturals" is ח (cheth), not ה: the left stroke joins the top bar, and the sense requires it — Gesenius is contrasting the *stronger* gutturals ח and ע with the weaker ה and א into which they soften.

Both foreign words are printed in sloping Serto Syriac type (long diagonal final lamadh, Syriac points above), not Arabic. B is right that the first is Syriac ܐܶܬܩܰܛܰܠ, but both A and B wrongly give the second as Arabic أَقْتَلَ; it is Syriac ܐܰܩܛܶܠ.

Three vowel marks are printed over the Syriac word: a small stroke (pthaha) above the he as well as the two zqapha rings over the beths, so Reading A's ܗܰ is correct and B's unpointed he is wrong. (The thin gap before the final semicolon in the print is 19th‑c. typographic spacing, not a distinct character.)
The first (leftmost) word is printed כָּאָה (kaph with dagesh, aleph, he), paralleling כָּהָה — not אָגַם, which appears only at the line end. Reading B matches every letter and point.
The first word is printed in Syriac Serto script with vowel points above it (ܝܠܦ, "to learn"), not Arabic أَلِفَ as in Reading B; the Hebrew items and their order agree in both.
The aleph carries a holem dot printed above it, not a tsere beneath — the point is בֹּור for בְּאֹר (the vav being the quiescent for holem), so Reading A's אֹ is right and B's אֵ is wrong.
The first Hebrew item printed (left) begins with א (aleph + hataf patah), i.e. the full form אֲנַחְנוּ; the shorter aphæretic form נַחְנוּ comes second. Reading A reverses the order.

A raised dot is clearly printed immediately after (to the left of) the שֶׁ, Gesenius's usual mark for an inseparable prefix; Reading A omits it. Vowels (segol under shin, shin dot; אֶחָד with segol/qamets; חַד with patach) are identical in both readings and match the print.
The first Hebrew word is printed plene: a yod is clearly visible between the ṭet (with dagesh) and the ḥet — אֲבַטִּיחִים, as in Reading B; Reading A drops that yod.

Printed left-to-right order is אֲבַעְבּוּעֹת first (leftmost), then אֲדַרְכּוֹן (as B), but the first word is plene with shureq vav בּוּ (as A), not kubbutz בֻּ. Each reading gets one point right, so neither is fully correct.

Under the initial pe (which has a dagesh) the print shows two vertically stacked dots, i.e. shewa, not the three-dot segol of Reading A; this matches the paragraph's point (prosthetic aleph before a movable shewa) and the preceding line's אֶפְרוֹחַ. The rest (אֶגְרֹף, גֹּרֶף with dagesh and holem on gimel, segol under resh) is identical in both readings and matches the print.
Under the tav of the second word the print shows two vertically stacked dots (sheva) with a dagesh in the letter, not a qamets; so תְּנָן (B), not תָּנָן (A). All other items agree with the print.
